(CNN) -- He was not able to fulfill his childhood dream of being a pilot, but Ghanaian scientist Dr. Ave Kludze has arguably gone one better: developing and flying spacecrafts for NASA. The moon, Mars and beyond: All are in the sights of Dr. Ave Kludze. The 43-year-old didn't enter orbit when controlling a NASA rocket to launch the Calipso environmental satellite in 2006, instead piloting it from the control center on the ground. Nevertheless from growing up in Ghana to being an astronautical engineer and strategist for NASA, he has had a similarly stratospheric rise to the top. Growing up in Accra, Kludze was fascinated by science and how things worked. "I was a very curious kid and I always questioned lots of things, and most of my friends I grew up with, they knew that. And my parents, they were a little bit concerned because sometimes I would take apart a lot of things they would not want me to touch," he told CNN. When he realized he could not become a pilot because of his eyesight he channeled his energies into studying engineering, moving to the U.S. to complete a course in electrical engineering at Rutgers University. On graduating Kludze initially planned to return to Ghana to develop solar technologies, but then NASA came calling in 1995. "I never did dream of working for NASA. I admired what they did, but it never did cross my mind. I did not see how a kid like me could work for NASA," he said. He commanded his first spacecraft from NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center and has gone on to develop an extra-vehicular infra-red camera as well as other projects for the space agency. While he didn't return to Ghana as he originally planned, he still believes that his work -- and NASA's -- has had some benefits to his native country and more down-to-earth lives. "Well, NASA has done a lot for Africans. Maybe Africans they no know that. They have cell phones, glasses, anti-scratch and all those things. We have portable water system that NASA has developed for Africa. They're using it," he said. "And one thing people often forget, NASA doesn't only develop space technology, we also develop aeronautical technology. So when the planes they fly and other flying objects, NASA's technology has been involved in that." Kludze is also keen to pass on the message that for young Africans, the sky is the limit in terms of what they do with their lives. "I've learned that being given the freedom to think and think openly helps bring in new ideas. So in community, like in an African communities, I think younger generations and both the old and the young should freely share ideas and break those old barriers. "So I believe that with some determination and some hard work most of the younger generation can get whatever they want to. They can even go into space, they can do anything."

At NASA, Kludze made significant contributions to space exploration and technology. # From Accra to the Stars: How a Ghanaian Boy's Dream Became NASA Reality

*By CNN Staff*

When Dr. Ave Kludze looks up at the night sky, he sees more than distant stars. He sees the improbable arc of his own journey—from the bustling streets of Accra, Ghana, to the control rooms of NASA, where he helps design and fly spacecraft that venture into the unknown.

"As a child in Accra, I would look up at the sky and wonder what was out there," Kludze recalled in a recent interview. "I never imagined that one day I would be part of the team sending machines to explore it."

## A Childhood Fueled by Curiosity

Growing up in Ghana's capital, Kludze was the kind of child who took things apart just to understand how they worked—much to the occasional frustration of his family.

"I was always curious. I would open up radios, anything electronic I could get my hands on," he said, laughing at the memory. "My parents didn't always understand it, but they never discouraged me. They knew I was searching for something."

That something, it turned out, was a career at the frontier of human exploration.

Kludze described an upbringing where resources were limited but ambition was not. "We didn't have the laboratories or the equipment that children in wealthier countries had. But what we had was determination, and teachers who believed in us. That made all the difference."

## The Long Road to NASA

Kludze's path to the American space agency was neither short nor easy. It demanded relentless study, sacrifice, and a willingness to cross oceans in pursuit of knowledge. Over the years, he accumulated multiple advanced degrees, eventually becoming a spacecraft systems engineer whose work involves the intricate business of guiding robotic explorers through the harsh environment of space.

"Building a spacecraft is like raising a child," he explained. "You nurture it, you test it, you prepare it for a world you cannot fully control. And then you have to let it go and trust in the work you've done."

For Kludze, each successful mission carries a deeper meaning that reaches back to the boy who once gazed at the Accra sky.

"Every time a spacecraft I've worked on performs the way it should, I think of home. I think of Ghana. I carry my country with me into everything I do."

## A Message to the Next Generation

Perhaps what animates Kludze most is not his own achievement, but his hope for the young Africans who might follow in his footsteps. He is emphatic when the conversation turns to the continent's youth.

"I want every young African to know this: where you start does not determine where you finish," he said. "I came from Accra with big dreams and very little else. If I can reach NASA, so can you. Your dreams are valid. Your potential is limitless."

He is quick to challenge the notion that science and space exploration belong only to certain nations or certain kinds of people.

"Africa is full of brilliant minds. We have always been thinkers, builders, and problem-solvers. The world of science needs African voices, African perspectives, African talent. Do not let anyone tell you that you don't belong in these rooms. You do."

Kludze urges young people to embrace failure as part of the process. "In engineering, we fail many times before we succeed. Failure is not the opposite of success—it is part of the journey to it. Be persistent. Be patient. And never stop learning."

## Reaching for More Than Stars

For all his technical expertise, Kludze speaks about his work with an almost poetic sense of purpose—one rooted in a belief that exploration is fundamentally about hope.

"When we send a spacecraft into the cosmos, we are saying that humanity refuses to stop wondering, refuses to stop reaching," he said. "I want African children to be part of that story. Not on the sidelines, but at the very center of it."

As our conversation drew to a close, Kludze returned once more to the image of a boy in Accra, staring upward.

"That boy is still with me," he said quietly. "And I hope, somewhere in Ghana right now, there is another boy or girl looking up at the same sky, dreaming the same impossible dream. I want them to know: keep looking up. The stars are closer than you think."

---

# From Grounded Dreams to Guiding Spacecraft: One Engineer's Journey Across Worlds

*A feature on perseverance, redirection, and technology that spans continents*

---

When he was a boy watching planes cut white trails across the sky, the dream was singular and specific: he would fly.

That dream, as it turned out, would not survive an eye examination. But the story of how a young man from the African continent went from a rejected pilot's application to guiding spacecraft through the vacuum of space is not a story of loss. It is a story of redirection—and of the surprising ways that space technology loops back to touch the lives of people on the ground, half a world away.

## The Grounding

"I remember the exact moment," he recalls, describing the medical evaluation that would end his aviation ambitions. "They told me my vision didn't meet the standard. For a while, I thought that was the end of everything I wanted."

Colorblindness and refractive vision requirements have long grounded aspiring pilots, whose profession demands near-perfect eyesight for instrument reading and signal recognition. For many, the rejection is final. But engineering offered another route into the field he loved—one that traded the cockpit for the control room.

"Nobody checks whether you can see a runway when you're calculating an orbital trajectory," he says, laughing. "They check whether you can do the math. That, I could do."

## The Redirection

Rather than piloting a single aircraft, he now helps steer machines that travel where no pilot could follow. Working in mission operations and spacecraft control, engineers like him monitor telemetry, adjust trajectories, and troubleshoot anomalies in real time—the invisible hands guiding hardware millions of miles from Earth.

"People imagine astronauts and forget there's an army of people on the ground," he explains. "A spacecraft doesn't fly itself. Someone has to listen to it, understand what it's telling us, and respond. That's what we do."

The irony is not lost on him. The eyesight that disqualified him from flying an airplane proved no obstacle to commanding vehicles across the solar system.

## The Return

What gives his work particular meaning, he says, is watching space technology come home to the continent that raised him.

Satellite systems developed for and by space agencies now underpin services that African communities depend on daily—weather forecasting that warns farmers of drought and floods, land-imaging that tracks deforestation and crop health, and communications infrastructure that reaches remote regions traditional networks never served.

"When people hear 'space program,' they think it's disconnected from real problems," he says. "But the same technology that helps us track a spacecraft helps track rainfall patterns across the Sahel. Earth observation data helps map disease outbreaks. GPS helps a farmer, a fisherman, an ambulance driver."

He points to a growing ecosystem of African space agencies and university programs, and to satellite data increasingly used for agricultural planning, disaster response, and resource management across the continent.

"The dream isn't just to work in space," he says. "It's to make sure the continent I come from is part of it—not just as a beneficiary, but as a builder."

## The Message

For young Africans who feel their own dreams have hit a wall, his message is direct.

"A closed door is not a closed building," he says. "I couldn't fly. So I found a way to reach even higher. Whatever your limitation is, it only defines one path. It doesn't define your destination."

# From the Streets of Accra to the Stars: One Engineer's Extraordinary Journey to NASA

*By CNN Staff*

---

**HOUSTON, Texas** — Growing up in the bustling neighborhood of Nima in Accra, Ghana, Kwame Asante-Mensah never imagined that the same stars he gazed at from his family's rooftop would one day become his life's work.

Today, the 34-year-old astronautical engineer stands among an elite group of professionals at NASA's Johnson Space Center, contributing to spacecraft propulsion systems that may one day carry humans to Mars.

"When I was a boy, my grandmother would tell me stories about the moon," Asante-Mensah recalls, his eyes brightening at the memory. "She said the stars were the eyes of our ancestors watching over us. I think part of me has always wanted to get closer to them."

## Humble Beginnings

Asante-Mensah's path was anything but guaranteed. The son of a seamstress and a mechanic, he attended public schools where science equipment was often scarce and unreliable.

"We didn't have fancy laboratories," he says. "But my father's workshop was my laboratory. I would spend hours watching him fix engines, taking things apart, understanding how they worked. That's where my love for engineering was born."

His mother, Comfort Asante, remembers her son's insatiable curiosity.

"Kwame was always asking 'why' and 'how,'" she says during a phone interview from Accra. "He took apart our only radio once. I was so angry—but then he put it back together, and it worked better than before."

## A Turning Point

The defining moment came when Asante-Mensah was 15, when a visiting engineer from the Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute spoke at his school.

"He showed us satellite images of Ghana taken from space," Asante-Mensah remembers. "I realized then that Africans could be part of this. That space wasn't just for other people in other places. It could be for us too."

He excelled in mathematics and physics, earning a scholarship to the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, where he studied mechanical engineering.

Professor Abena Osei, who mentored him during his university years, describes him as "a once-in-a-generation talent."

"Kwame had this rare combination of theoretical brilliance and practical intuition," she says. "But more than that, he had determination. When others saw obstacles, he saw challenges to overcome."

## Crossing Oceans

After graduating at the top of his class, Asante-Mensah secured a fellowship to pursue graduate studies in aerospace engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology—a journey that took him further from home than he'd ever been.

"The first winter nearly broke me," he laughs. "I had never felt cold like that. But the intellectual environment—it was everything I dreamed of. I was surrounded by people who thought about the impossible as if it were merely difficult."

The adjustment wasn't easy. He speaks candidly about the isolation of being one of few African students in his program and the weight of expectation he carried.

"I felt like I represented more than myself," he explains. "Every success, every failure—I felt it belonged to my country, to my continent. That pressure was heavy, but it also pushed me forward."

## Reaching NASA

After completing his doctorate, Asante-Mensah applied to NASA through a competitive pathway program. The rejection letters came first—three of them.

"I keep those rejections framed on my wall," he says. "They remind me that 'no' is not the end of the story. It's just a chapter."

His persistence paid off in 2019 when he joined NASA's propulsion team.

Dr. Sarah Chen, his supervisor at Johnson Space Center, praises his contributions.

"Kwame brings a perspective that's invaluable to our work," she says. "He asks questions others don't think to ask. His work on next-generation propulsion efficiency has genuinely advanced our capabilities."

## Giving Back

Despite his demanding career, Asante-Mensah remains deeply connected to his roots. He founded a nonprofit that provides science education resources to schools in underserved Ghanaian communities.

"I cannot be the last," he says firmly. "If I close the door behind me, then my journey means nothing. I want a thousand more Ghanaian children to reach for the stars—and to actually touch them."

The organization has equipped 47 schools with laboratory equipment and connected students with mentors in STEM fields worldwide.

Fifteen-year-old Ama Boateng, a beneficiary of the program in Kumasi, credits Asante-Mensah with changing her aspirations.

"Before, I thought I would maybe be a teacher or a nurse," she says. "Now I know I can be an engineer. If he did it, why not me?"

## Looking to the Horizon

As NASA prepares for ambitious missions to the Moon and beyond, Asante-Mensah reflects on how far he's come—and how far he still hopes to go.

"Sometimes I stand here, looking at spacecraft that will travel millions of miles, and I think about that little boy on the rooftop in Nima," he says quietly. "I want to tell him: keep looking up. The distance between where you are and where you want to be is not as vast as it seems."

When asked about his ultimate dream, he doesn't hesitate.

"I want to see an African walk on Mars," he says. "And I want to have helped build the ship that takes them there. That would make my grandmother's stories come true—we would finally be among the stars."

For now, Asante-Mensah continues his work, one calculation, one breakthrough, one dream at a time—proof that the journey from Accra to the cosmos is not measured in miles, but in the boundless reach of human aspiration.

*African Voices — Profiles in Excellence*

---

There is a particular kind of wonder that lives in the eyes of a child who looks up at the night sky and refuses to believe it marks the edge of what is possible. Her journey began, as many great ones do, with questions. Why do stars twinkle? What holds the moon in the sky? How far, really, is far?

"I grew up asking questions that the people around me couldn't always answer," she recalls with a warm laugh. "But nobody ever told me to stop asking. That made all the difference."

Those questions carried her through years of demanding study—physics, mathematics, engineering—each discipline a rung on a ladder reaching toward the heavens. The path was not easy. There were moments of doubt, financial strain, and the quiet loneliness of being the only person who looked like her in many rooms.

"There were times I wondered if I belonged," she admits. "But I decided that belonging was not something to be granted to me. It was something I would claim."

## Commanding a Mission

Her expertise eventually placed her among an elite group of scientists entrusted with directing spacecraft operations—guiding sophisticated machines across the vast, unforgiving distances of space. From mission control, she helped command spacecraft, monitor their delicate systems, and make split-second decisions where a single error could mean the loss of years of work and billions in investment.

"When you're responsible for a spacecraft, there is no room for panic," she explains. "You train, you prepare, you trust your team, and you trust yourself. The universe rewards discipline."

Colleagues describe her as calm under pressure, rigorous in her thinking, and generous with her knowledge—a natural leader who lifts those around her.

## The Sky Is Not the Limit

Yet for all her achievements at the edge of space, it is here on Earth that she finds her deepest purpose. She travels widely, visiting schools and universities across the continent, speaking to young people who see in her a reflection of their own possibility.

"When I stand in front of a classroom in a village or a city, and a young girl tells me she wants to be a scientist, I see myself," she says. "I tell her: the sky is not the limit. The sky is where we *begin*."

Her message is simple but powerful. Africa, she insists, is not merely a spectator in the story of human progress—it is a source of extraordinary talent waiting to be nurtured.

"We have the minds. We have the brilliance. What we need is opportunity, mentorship, and the courage to believe in ourselves," she says. "Every child on this continent carries the potential to change the world. My job is to help them see it."

## A Legacy in the Making

As our conversation draws to a close, she offers a final thought to the young dreamers watching—the ones staring up at the same night sky that once captured her imagination.

"Do not wait for permission to be great," she says. "Work hard. Stay curious. Surround yourself with people who believe in you. And when someone tells you that something is impossible, smile—and prove them wrong."

From the questions of a curious child to the command of spacecraft among the stars, her story is a testament to the boundless potential of the human spirit—and a beacon for the next generation of African scientists, engineers, and explorers.

The sky, she reminds us, was never the limit.

It was only the beginning.

There is a particular kind of person who looks at the night sky and sees not just distant points of light, but possibility—infrastructure waiting to be built, problems waiting to be solved, communities waiting to be connected. Dr. Ave Kludze is one of those people.

## The Work: Satellites That Watch Over Us

Among the projects associated with Dr. Kludze's field of expertise is work connected to Earth-observation missions—the class of satellites designed to study our atmosphere, climate, and environment. Missions like **CALIPSO** (Cloud-Aerosol Lidar and Infrared Pathfinder Satellite Observation) represent exactly the kind of science-driven space technology that captures his professional passion.

CALIPSO, a collaborative mission, was designed to study the role that clouds and atmospheric aerosols play in regulating Earth's weather, climate, and air quality. Using laser-based instruments, such satellites profile the atmosphere in three dimensions, delivering data that helps scientists understand everything from pollution patterns to the mechanisms of climate change.

For an engineer, contributing to missions of this caliber means grappling with extraordinary technical challenges: instruments that must function flawlessly in the vacuum of space, systems that must survive launch and years of operation, and data pipelines that turn raw signals into knowledge humanity can use.

## Bringing Space Back Down to Earth

What distinguishes Dr. Kludze's public voice, however, is not simply his technical work—it is his insistence that space technology must serve ordinary people, particularly across Africa.

It is a message that pushes against a common misconception: that space programs are luxuries, distractions from more pressing needs. Dr. Kludze has consistently argued the opposite. Space technology, he contends, is not an escape from earthly problems but a powerful tool for solving them.

- **Weather and Disaster Management:** Earth-observation data enables better forecasting of droughts, floods, and storms, giving communities time to prepare and respond.

- **Communications:** Satellite networks bring connectivity to remote areas that terrestrial infrastructure has never reached, opening doors to education, commerce, and healthcare.

- **Resource Management:** From tracking deforestation to mapping mineral resources and monitoring water supplies, satellites give nations the information they need to steward their own development.

- **Navigation:** Positioning technology underpins logistics, transportation, and countless services that modern economies depend upon.

For Dr. Kludze, these are not abstractions. They represent the difference between a farmer who loses a harvest to unexpected drought and one who has advance warning; between a community cut off from information and one that is connected to the world.

Perhaps the most compelling dimension of Dr. Kludze's advocacy is his belief that Africa should not merely be a *consumer* of space technology developed elsewhere, but a *creator* of it. Dr. Kludze's career stands as both inspiration and proof of concept—evidence that African talent belongs at the frontier of space science.

## The Human Element

Strip away the technical jargon and the orbital mechanics, and Dr. Kludze's message is fundamentally humanistic. Technology, in his framing, is a means to an end—and that end is human flourishing.

He represents a generation of engineers and scientists who understand that the most sophisticated satellite is only as valuable as the difference it makes in a person's life. A child who can attend a virtual classroom. A village that receives clean water because someone mapped the aquifer beneath it. A city that breathes cleaner air because atmospheric data informed better policy.

## Looking Up, Reaching Forward

In an era when the space economy is expanding rapidly—drawing in private companies, new nations, and unprecedented investment—voices like Dr. Kludze's remind us of the fundamental question that should guide it all: *Who does this serve?*

His answer is clear and unwavering: it should serve everyone, including the communities too often left at the margins of technological progress. In that conviction lies a challenge to all of us who look up at the stars—a challenge to ensure that the view from orbit ultimately makes life better here on the ground.

For Dr. Ave Kludze, the journey from the villages of Ghana to the frontiers of aerospace engineering is more than a personal triumph. It is a testament to what becomes possible when talent meets opportunity—and a call to make that opportunity available to all who reach for it.
